name: The Fork
aka: The Double Attack by a Knight
summary: One knight attacks the king and queen at once, so the king moves and the queen falls next turn
intro: A fork is a single piece that attacks two or more of the opponent's pieces on the same move. Because only one threat can be answered, the other target is lost. The knight is the classic forker: its jump cannot be blocked or interposed, and it strikes squares no other piece covers. Every improving player learns to hunt for forks first.
boardCaption: White knight on b5 leaps to c7, checking the king on e8 while also attacking the queen on d5 in a devastating royal fork.

sections.heading: What a Fork Is
paragraphs: A fork happens when one piece menaces two targets simultaneously. The defender can only parry a single threat per move, so at least one attacked piece is doomed. When one of the two targets is the king, the check must be met first, guaranteeing the other target cannot be saved. This special case is called a royal fork, and it is usually decisive.

Knights fork more often than any other piece because their movement is unique. Bishops, rooks, and queens attack along straight lines that can be blocked by interposing a piece. A knight's attack cannot be interposed at all, and it reaches squares of the opposite colour to the ones it stands on, making its double attacks hard to foresee and impossible to shield.

sections.heading: The Line Move by Move
paragraphs: White begins with 1.Nc7+, planting the knight where it forks the black king on e8 and the queen on d5 at the same instant. This is a royal fork: the check on the king takes absolute priority, so Black has no time to rescue the queen. Every other piece is irrelevant while the king stands in check.

Black must address the check, and the king steps to safety with 1...Kd8. The queen, however, is still attacked by the knight and has not moved. White simply harvests it with 2.Nxd5, emerging a full queen ahead. The whole combination rests on the fact that a check cannot be ignored, converting a double attack into a clean win of material.

sections.heading: How to Spot Forks
paragraphs: Train your eye to notice enemy pieces that share a knight's-move relationship, especially the king and queen. Undefended or loosely guarded pieces are prime fork targets, so scan the board for squares from which one leap hits two of them. Checks that also strike a second piece deserve a hard look, since the forced reply hands you the second target.

When you are the defender, keep your king and queen off squares a single knight can attack together, and watch for enemy knights arriving near your camp. Giving loose pieces a guard removes many forking chances. Before every move, ask whether the piece you are about to leave undefended could be forked alongside your king on the next turn.

keyIdeas: A fork is one piece attacking two or more targets at once.
The knight forks best because its attack cannot be blocked or interposed.
A royal fork hits the king and queen together and is usually winning.
The check must be answered first, so the second target cannot escape.
Loose or undefended pieces are the most common fork victims.
Keep your king and queen off squares one knight can hit together.
